<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
Suppose that $\mathcal{F}$ is a hereditary family of subsets of $\omega_1$. Denote $K = \overline{\mathcal{F}}$. Then
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $K$ is not first countable,
		\item $\mathcal{F}$ is a Corson family iff there exists no continuous surjection $f\colon K \to [0,1]^{\omega_1}$,
		\item $\mathcal{F}$ is a Corson family iff  $K$ is Corson compact.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
(1) Notice that $\emptyset$ does not have a countable base.
	\medskip

	(2 $\impliedby$). Suppose that $\mathcal{F}$ is not a Corson family and that $I\subseteq \kappa$ is a set of size $\omega_1$ from $\overline{\mathcal{F}}$. Let $g\colon K \to \{0,1\}^{I}$ be defined by $g(x) = x|I$. Then $g$ is
	a continuous surjection and $\{0,1\}^I$ can be continuously transformed onto $[0,1]^{\omega_1}$. 
	\medskip

	(3 $\implies$). If $\mathcal{F}$ is Corson, then  $K\subseteq \Sigma_\kappa(\{0,1\})$.
	\medskip

	(3 $\impliedby$) Note that Corson compacta cannot be mapped continuously onto $[0, 1]^{\omega_1}.$ By (2 $\impliedby$) if $\mathcal{F}$ is not a Corson family, there exists a surjection, hence $K$ is not a Corson compact.
    \medskip
    
    (2 $\implies$) If $\mathcal{F}$ is Corson, then by (3 $\implies$) $K$ is a Corson compact, so such surjection cannot exist.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{C(F)}
    Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a hereditary family on $\kappa$. Then $X_\mathcal{F}$ is a closed subspace of $C(\overline{\mathcal{F}})$.
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The most natural mapping $T\colon X_\mathcal{F} \to C(\overline{\mathcal{F}})$, defined by \[ Tx (A) = \sum_{\alpha \in A} x(\alpha), \] works. Since every $x$ has a countable support and is absolutely convergent, $Tx$ yields a well defined function on $\overline{\mathcal{F}}$.
	We shall check that this function is continuous. Pick $\varepsilon > 0$. Then let $x_0$ be an element of $c_{00}(\kappa)$ with $\|x_0 - x\| <\varepsilon.$ Let $S$ be a support of $x_0$. Then pick $A, B \in \overline{\mathcal{F}}$ satisfying $A\cap S = B\cap S$. We have 

	\begin{align*}
            |Tx(A) - Tx(B)| = & \bigg | \sum_{\alpha \in A\Delta B} x(\alpha) \bigg | \leq \sum_{\alpha \in A \Delta B} |x(\alpha)| = \sum_{A\backslash B} |x(\alpha)| + \sum_{B\backslash A} |x(\alpha)| = \\
			& \leq \sum_{B \backslash S} |x(\alpha)| + \sum_{A \backslash S} |x(\alpha)| \leq 2 \|x - x_0\|_\mathcal{F} \leq 2\varepsilon.
    \end{align*}
	
	Now we will check that $T$ itself is continuous.	Obviously, we have $\|Tx\|_\infty \leq \|x\|_\mathcal{F}$.
    Now, pick $A \in \overline{\mathcal{F}}$. Let $A_+ = \{\alpha \in A: x(\alpha) > 0\}, A_-= \{\alpha \in A: x(\alpha) < 0\}$. We have \[
    \sum_{\alpha \in A} |x(\alpha)| \leq \bigg |\sum_{\alpha\in A_+} x(\alpha) \bigg | + \bigg | \sum_{\alpha \in A_-} x(\alpha) \bigg | \leq 2 \| Tx\|_\infty,
\]so $\frac{1}{2} \| x\|_\mathcal{F} \leq \|Tx\|_\infty.$
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{countable-support-in-*}
Let $c$ be a coloring on $\kappa>\omega$. Then $c$ does not have an uncountable $1$-monochromatic set iff every functional from $X^*_c$ has a countable support.
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Suppose first that there is $I\subseteq \kappa$ of size $\omega_1$ which is $1$-monochromatic for $c$. Then $\varphi = \chi_I \in X^*_c$. 

	Assume now that there is $\varphi\in X_c^*$ and an uncountable set $I\subseteq \kappa$ such that $\varphi(e_\alpha)\neq 0$ for $\alpha\in I$. We may assume that $\|\varphi\|^*_c =1$. By shrinking $I$ and replacing $\varphi$ with $-\varphi$ if necessary we may also assume that there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that $\varphi(e_\alpha)>\varepsilon$ for $\alpha\in I$.

	Since we assumed that $I$ has no uncountable $1$-monochromatic subsets, by the Erd\H{o}s--Dushnik--Miller theorem there is an infinite $0$-monochromatic $J\subseteq I$. Pick $n>\frac{1}{\varepsilon}$, take $A\subseteq J$ of size $n$ and consider
$x=\chi_A$. Then $\|x\|_c=\|x\|_\infty=1$ and $\varphi(x) > n\varepsilon > 1$, which contradicts the fact that $\|\varphi\|^*_c=1$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
Suppose $\mathcal{F} \subseteq [\kappa]^{<\omega}$ is a family such that for every uncountable $S\subseteq \kappa$ the family $\mathcal{F}^\perp|S$ is not bounded. Then every functional from $X^*_\mathcal{F}$ has a countable support.
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
By way of contradiction assume that there is $\varphi\in X_\mathcal{F}^*$ with an uncountable support and that $X^*_\mathcal{F}$ satisfies condition in the statement. Let $I\subseteq \kappa$ be an uncountable subset of $\operatorname{supp}(\varphi)$. We may assume that $\|\varphi\|^*_\mathcal{F} =1$ and that there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that $\varphi(e_\alpha)>\varepsilon$ for $\alpha\in I$. Now, pick $n>\frac{1}{\varepsilon}$, take any $n$-element $A\subseteq I$, $A\in \mathcal{F}^\perp$ and consider
    $x=\chi_A$. Then $\|x\|_\mathcal{F}=\|x\|_\infty=1$ and $\varphi(x) > n\varepsilon > 1$, which contradicts the fact that $\|\varphi\|^*_\mathcal{F}=1$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label{countable-support-in-Y}
Let $c$ be a coloring of $\kappa>\omega$ without uncountable $0$-monochro-matic sets. Then every $x\in Y_c$ has a countable support.
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Assume that there is $x\in Y_c$ with an uncountable support. Let $A\subseteq \operatorname{supp}(x)$ be such that for some $\varepsilon>0$ we have $x(\alpha)>\varepsilon$ for every $\alpha\in A$. By the Erd\H{o}s--Dushnik--Miller theorem there is an infinite $1$-monochromatic $B\subseteq A$. Then clearly 
    $$\|x\|_c \geq \|P_B x\|_c = \|P_B x\|_1 \geq \sum_{\alpha\in B} x(\alpha) = +\infty,$$
    which yields a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{F}\subseteq [\kappa]^{<\omega}$ be such that $\mathcal{F}$ is not bounded on any uncountable set.
Then every $x\in Y_\mathcal{F}$ has a countable support.
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- rem-1: body_md -->
Note that for a monochromatic family $\mathcal{F}\subseteq [\kappa]^{<\omega}$  the following are equivalent: 
\begin{enumerate}
	\item There is a set $S\in [\kappa]^\kappa$ such that $\mathcal{F}|S$ is bounded,
\item There is a 0-monochromatic set of size $\kappa$.
\end{enumerate}
Indeed, $2)\Rightarrow 1)$ is obvious, for $1)\Rightarrow 2)$ note that by the Erd\H{o}s-Dushnik-Miller theorem either there is a $0$-monochromatic $S'\subseteq S$ of size $\kappa$, since there can be no infinite set in the closure of $\mathcal{F}|S$.
<!-- end rem-1 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{perfect}
Let $c$ be a perfect coloring of $\kappa > \omega$ without uncountable $1$-monochromatic sets. Then $X_c^* = Y_{1-c}$.
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Take $\varphi\in X_c^*$. By Proposition \ref{countable-support-in-*} it has a countable support $A\subseteq \kappa$. It allows us to view $\varphi$ as a functional on $X_d$, where $X_d$ is a separable combinatorial Banach space induced by
	$d=c|_{[A]^2}$. Since $d$ is a perfect coloring, it follows from \cite[Theorem 4.6]{Perfect} that $\varphi\in Y_{1-d}$, which implies that $\varphi\in Y_{1-c}$.

	Let now $\psi \in Y_{1-c}$. Since $1-c$ admits no uncountable $0$-monochromatic sets, by Proposition \ref{countable-support-in-Y} $\psi$ has a countable support $B\subseteq \kappa$. Let $e=c|_{[B]^2}$. Clearly we may view $\psi$ as an element of $Y_{1-e}$. Since $e$ is perfect, $\psi \in X_e^*$ and its natural extension belongs to $X_c^*$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- prop-7: body_md -->
\label{l1-separable} Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a hereditary family on $\omega$. Then, the following conditions are equivalent:
	\begin{enumerate}
	\item $\overline{\mathcal{F}}$ contains an infinite set,
	\item $X_\mathcal{F}$ contains a copy of $\ell_1$,
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-7 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{calculus} Suppose that $\mu$ is a probability measure on $X$ and $f\colon X\to [0,\infty)$ is a $\mu$-measurable function bounded by $M$ and such that $\mu(f)=E$. Then
	\[ \mu(\{t\in X\colon f(t) \geq E/2\}) \geq E/2M. \]
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Let $X_0 = \{t\in X\colon f(t) \geq E/2\}$. Then $\mu(f) = \mu(f|X_0) + \mu(f|(X\setminus X_0))$ and so 
	\[ E \leq M\mu(X_0) + (E/2)(1-\mu(X_0)). \]
Performing rather straightforward calculations, using the fact that $M\geq M-E/2$, we get
\[ \mu(X_0) \geq E/2M. \]
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{measure-theory}
Suppose that $\mu$ is a probability measure on $2^\kappa$ and that $(A_n)_n$ is a family of measurable subsets of $2^{\kappa}$ such that $\mu(A_n)>\delta$ for some $\delta>0$ and every $n$. Let $x$ be a bounded sequence of positive reals such that $\sum_i x(i) = \infty$. Then there is $t\in 2^{\kappa}$ such that $\sum_{i\in B_t} x(i) = \infty$, where $B_t = \{n\colon t\in A_n\}$.
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Note that $1\geq \delta$. For $n\in \omega$ and $t\in 2^\kappa$ let $T_n = \sum_{i\leq n} x(i)$ and let $$S_n(t) = \sum_{i\leq B_t \cap [0, ..., n]} x(i) = \sum_{i\leq n} x(i)\chi_{A_i}(t).$$
	Fix $n > 0$. Now let $X_n = \{t\in 2^\kappa \colon S_n(t) \geq \delta T_n / 2 \}$. We have $\mu(S_n)> \delta T_n$ and $S_n(x) \leq T_n$. 
	Applying Lemma \ref{calculus} to $S_n$ we get
	\[ \mu(X_n) \geq \mu(\{t\colon S_n \geq \mu(S_n)/2\}) \geq \mu(S_n)/2T_n > \delta/2. \]
	Now let $X = \bigcap_n \bigcup_{m>n} X_m$ and notice that $\mu(X)\geq \delta/2$, in particular it is nonempty. But if $t\in X$, then $\sum_{i\in A_t} x(i) = \infty$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{l1-general} Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a hereditary family on $\kappa$ and let $\lambda\leq \kappa$. Suppose that $cf(\lambda) > \omega$. The following conditions are equivalent:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item The space $\overline{\mathcal{F}}$ carries a measure $\mu$ of type at least $\lambda$.
		\item The space $X_\mathcal{F}$ contains a copy of $\ell_1(\lambda)$.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
(1) $\implies$ (2). Let $K_\alpha$ be defined as at the beginning of the section. Then there exists a number $\delta > 0$ such that 
    $|\{\alpha <\kappa: \mu(K_\alpha) >\delta\}| \geq \lambda.$
    Suppose this is not the case, then for every $n$ the set $\{\alpha < \kappa: \mu(K_\alpha) > 1/n\}$ has cardinality smaller than $\lambda$. By uncountable cofinality of $\lambda$ we get that $|\{\alpha <\kappa: \mu(K_\alpha) > 0\}| < \lambda$. Hence, the family of clopen subsets of $\overline{\mathcal{F}}$ whose coordinates depend on $N$ is dense and so $\mu$ is of type less than $\lambda$. 
    We claim that the basic sequence $(e_\alpha)_{\alpha \in I}$ in $X_\mathcal{F}$ is equivalent to the standard basis of $\ell_1(\lambda)$. Suppose not. Then we have the following:
	\medskip

	\textbf{Claim.} There is a (necessarily bounded) positive $x$ with the support in $I$ such that $\|x\|_\mathcal{F}<\infty$ but $\|x\|_1= \infty$. 
	\medskip

	Indeed, for each $k\in \omega$ we may find $x_k$ such that $\|x_k\|_\mathcal{F}<1/2^k$, $\|x_k\|_1 = 1$, and the support of $x_k$ is a finite subset of $I$. We may also assume that the supports of $x_k$ are pairwise disjoint. Then $x = \sum_k
	x_k$ is as required.
	\medskip


    By Lemma \ref{measure-theory} we may find $M\subseteq \mathrm{supp}(x)$, $M \in \overline{\mathcal{F}}$ such that $\sum_{i\in M} x(i) = \infty$. But it would mean that $\| x\|_\mathcal{F} = \infty$, a contradiction.
	\medskip

	(2) $\implies$ (1). It follows directly from Proposition \ref{C(F)} and a result due to Pe\l czynski (\cite{Pelczynski68}, see also \cite{Plebanek02}) saying that if a Banach space $X$ contains a copy of $\ell_1(\lambda)$, then $X^*$ contains a copy of
	$L_1(\mu_\lambda)$, where $\mu_\lambda$ is
	the standard measure on $2^\lambda$. However, we will show a direct argument here. Suppose that
	$X_\mathcal{F}$ contains a copy of $\ell_1(\lambda)$. Then there is
	an injective operator $S\colon \ell_1(\lambda) \to C(K)$, where $K = \overline{\mathcal{F}}$ as $C(K)$ contains a closed copy of $X_\mathcal{F}$. So, there is a continuous surjective operator $T\colon C^*(K) \to \ell_1^*(\lambda)$. Thus, there is a
	continuous surjective operator $T\colon M(K) \to \ell_\infty(\lambda)$; here $M(K)$ stands for the space of signed, Radon measures on $K$. The operator
	is defined by $T(\mu)(x) = \int S(x) \ d\mu$. Let $\varphi$ be an  element of $\ell_\infty(\lambda)$ constantly equal 1 and let $\mu$ be such that $T(\mu) = \varphi$. 

	We will show that $\mu$ is of type $\lambda$.  Let $\alpha \ne \beta$. Then  \[ \| S(e_\alpha - e_\beta) \|_{L_1(\mu)} = \int | S(e_\alpha - e_\beta) |
	d\mu = \varphi(|e_\alpha - e_\beta|) = 2 . \]
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- rem-2: body_md -->
Let us comment on the connection between Proposition \ref{l1-separable} and Theorem \ref{l1-general}. In the separable case we have that $\overline{\mathcal{F}}$ contains an infinite set if and only if it is not scattered. By theorem
	of Rudin a compact space is scattered if and only if it does not carry a non-atomic measure. So, we might as well formulate the condition (1) in Proposition \ref{l1-separable} as ``$\overline{\mathcal{F}}$ carries a measure of infinite type''
	thus seeing Proposition \ref{l1-separable} as a particular case of Theorem \ref{l1-general}.
<!-- end rem-2 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a hereditary family on $\omega_1$. Then the space $X_\mathcal{F}$ contains a copy of $\ell_1(\omega_1)$ if and only if the space $\overline{\mathcal{F}}$ carries a non-separable measure $\mu$.
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{l_1} Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a hereditary family of subsets of $\omega_1$. The following are equivalent:
	\begin{enumerate}
	\item $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N}_{\omega_1}) > \omega_1$,
	\item $\mathcal{F}$ is Corson iff $X_\mathcal{F}$ does not contain an isomorphic copy of $\ell_1(\omega_1)$, 
    \item $\mathcal{F}$ is Corson iff $X_\mathcal{F}$ is  WLD,
    \item Pt\'ak's lemma holds true for $\omega_1$.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
(2) $\implies$ (1). Let $(N_\alpha)_{\alpha<\omega_1}$ be a family of subsets of $\{0,1\}^{\omega_1}$ such that $\lambda(N_\alpha)=0$ and $\bigcup_{\alpha<\omega_1} N_\alpha
	= 2^{\omega_1}$. For each $\alpha<\omega_1$ choose a compact set $K_\alpha \subseteq 2^{\omega_1}\setminus \bigcup_{\xi < \alpha} N_\xi$ whose measure is bigger than 1/2. Define $\mathcal{F} = \{I\in [\omega_1]^{<\omega}\colon
	\bigcap_{\alpha \in I} K_\alpha \ne \emptyset \}$. Then $\mathcal{F}$ is Corson, yet by the same argument argument as in the proof of Theorem \ref{l1-general} it is isomorphic to $\ell_1(\omega_1)$. 
	\medskip

	(1) $\implies$ (2). It follows by Theorem \ref{l1-general} and by a theorem of Kunen and van Mill (\cite{KunenMill}) saying that a Corson compact space $K$ carries a non-separable measure if and only if $\mathrm{cov}(\mathcal{N}_{\omega_1}) = \omega_1$;
	\medskip

	(2) $\iff$ (3) is proved in \cite[Theorem 1.7]{Argyros93}	
	\medskip
	
	(2) $\implies$ (4): Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family such that 
	$$ \delta = \inf\{ \|x\|_\mathcal{F} :\ x\in c_{00}(\omega_1), x\geq 0, \|x\|_1=1\} >0.$$ Then for every $x\in c_{00}(\kappa)$, $x\geq 0$ we have
	$$\delta\|x\|_1 \leq \|x\|_\mathcal{F} \leq \|x\|_1,$$
	and consequently, since the standard basis of $X_\mathcal{F}$ is unconditional with constant 1, we have it for every $x\in c_{00}(\kappa)$. Therefore $\|\cdot\|_\mathcal{F}$ and $\| \cdot\|_1$ are equivalent and by (3) $\mathcal{F}$ is not Corson, so there is an uncountable set in $\overline{\mathcal{F}}$.
	\medskip
	
	(4)$\implies$ (2): Suppose there is a copy of $\ell_1(\omega_1)$ in $X_\mathcal{F}$. Then by a result of Drewnowski (see \cite{Drewnowski}) there is an uncountable set $\Gamma\subseteq \omega_1$ such that $(e_\alpha)_{\alpha\in \Gamma}$ is equivalent to the standard basis of $\ell_1(\Gamma)$. It follows that clearly $\mathcal{F}|\Gamma$ satisfies 
	$$\inf\{ \|x\|_\mathcal{F} :\ x\in c_{00}(\Gamma), x\geq 0, \|x\|_1=1\} >0$$
	and therefore, since Pt\'ak's lemma holds true for $\omega_1$, $\mathcal{F}$ is not Corson.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- prop-8: body_md -->
If $\mathcal{F}$ is monochromatic, then the following are equivalent:
	\begin{enumerate}
	\item $\mathcal{F}$ is Corson,
	\item $\ell_1(\omega_1)$ does not embed to $X_\mathcal{F}$.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-8 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
(2) $\implies$ (1) is obvious.
\medskip
	
(1) $\implies$ (2). Suppose that $X_\mathcal{F}$ contains an isomorphic copy of $\ell_1(\omega_1)$. By Theorem \ref{l_1} the space $X_\mathcal F$ is not WLD. Since the set $\{e_\alpha:\ \alpha<\omega_1\}$ is linearly dense in $X_\mathcal F$ and $X_\mathcal F$ is not WLD, it means there is a functional $\varphi\in X_\mathcal F^*$
with an uncountable support. By Proposition \ref{countable-support-in-*} this means that there is an uncountable $B\subseteq \kappa$ with $[B]^2\subseteq \mathcal F$ and so $\mathcal{F}$ is not Corson.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
(Plebanek) If $\kappa \geq \mathrm{cf}(\kappa)>\omega_1$, the following are equivalent for a compact space $K$:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item if $K$ carries a measure of type $\kappa$, then $K$ can be mapped continuously onto $[0,1]^\kappa$.
	\item $\kappa$ is a caliber of measure algebras. 
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
If $\kappa \geq \mathrm{cf}(\kappa)>\omega_1$, the following are equivalent for a family $\mathcal{F} \subseteq [\kappa]^{<\omega}$
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\ell_1(\kappa)$ can be embedded into $X_\mathcal{F}$ if and only if $\mathcal{F}$ which is not $\kappa$-Corson,
		\item $\kappa$ is a caliber of measure algebras.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- prop-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:c0} Let $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal and let $\mathcal{F} \subseteq [\kappa]^{<\omega}$. A space $X_\mathcal{F}$ is isomorphic to $c_0(\kappa)$ if and only if $\mathcal{F}$ is bounded. Consequently, $X_G$ is
	isomorphic to $c_0$ if and only if $G$ is $K_n$-free for some $n\in \omega$ (a graph is $K_n$-free if it does not contain a clique of size $n$).
<!-- end prop-9 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The only nontrivial part is to prove that if $X_\mathcal{F}$ is isomorphic to $c_0(\kappa)$, then $\sup\{|F|\colon F\in \mathcal{F}\}$ is finite. Suppose otherwise. Then there is a countable $I\subseteq
	\kappa$ such that $\sup\{|F|\colon F\in \mathcal{F}|I \} = \infty$, where $\mathcal{F}|I = \{F\cap I\colon F\in \mathcal{F}\}$. The space $X_{\mathcal{F}|I}$ is a closed complemented subpace of $X_\mathcal{F}$ which itself is isomorphic to
	$c_0(\kappa)$, and so $X_{\mathcal{F}|I}$ is isomorphic to $c_0$ (see \cite{Granero}). By the uniqueness of the base of $c_0$ (\cite{Zippin}, see also \cite[page 104]{ZOO}) we get a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- thm-5: body_md -->
\label{c0-general}
Let $\lambda \leq \kappa$ be infinite cardinals with $\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)>\omega$ and let $\mathcal{F} \subseteq [\kappa]^{<\omega}$ be a hereditary family covering $\kappa$.
The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item There is an isomorphic embedding $T\colon c_0(\lambda) \to X_\mathcal F$,
\item There is an operator $T\colon c_0(\lambda) \to X_\mathcal F$ with range of density $\lambda$,
\item There is $S\in [\kappa]^\lambda$ and $n<\omega$ such that $\mathcal F|S \subseteq [S]^{\leq n}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
$(1)\implies (2)$ is obvious. For $(3)\implies (1)$ just notice that for $x\in c_{00}(S)$ we have $\|x\|_\infty \leq \|x\| \leq n\|x\|_\infty$. We will prove $(2)\implies (3)$.
Let $T\colon c_0(\lambda) \to X_\mathcal F$ by an operator with range of density $\lambda$. We may assume that $\|T\|=1$. For $\lambda$-many $\alpha<\lambda$ the value $Te_\alpha$ is non-zero, therefore we may assume that this is the case for all $\alpha<\lambda$.
\medskip

\textbf{Claim.} The family $(\operatorname{supp}(Te_\alpha))_{\alpha<\lambda}$ is point-countable.
\medskip

Suppose this is not the case and find $\gamma<\kappa$ and $I\in [\lambda]^{\omega_1}$ such that for $\alpha\in I$ $$Te_\alpha(\gamma) \neq 0.$$
By passing to a subset we could further assume that there is $\varepsilon>0$ such that $|Te_\alpha(\gamma)|\geq \varepsilon$ and that for every $\alpha, \beta \in I$ the values $Te_\alpha(\gamma)$ and $Te_\beta(\gamma)$ have the same sign. Now pick $n<\omega$ large enough so that $n\varepsilon>1$ and distinct $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n \in I$ and note that
$$\|e_{\alpha_1} + e_{\alpha_2} + \ldots + e_{\alpha_n} \|_\infty =1$$
but
$$\|T(e_{\alpha_1} + e_{\alpha_2} + \ldots + e_{\alpha_n})\|\geq \|T(e_{\alpha_1} + e_{\alpha_2} + \ldots + e_{\alpha_n})\|_\infty \geq |T(e_{\alpha_1} + e_{\alpha_2} + \ldots + e_{\alpha_n})(\gamma)| = $$ $$|Te_{\alpha_1}(\gamma)| + \ldots + |Te_{\alpha_n}(\gamma)| > n\varepsilon>1,$$
which yields a contradiction.
\medskip

We may therefore assume that $(\operatorname{supp} Te_\alpha)_{\alpha<\lambda}$ are pairwise disjoint and, by further passing to a subset of $\lambda$ of size $\lambda$, that there is $n<\omega$ such that $\|Te_\alpha\|_\infty > 1/n$ for every
$\alpha<\lambda$. For every $\alpha<\lambda$ pick $\gamma_\alpha < \kappa$ such that $|Te_\alpha(\gamma_\alpha)| > 1/n$.

We claim that for $$S=\{\gamma_\alpha:\ \alpha<\lambda\}$$ we have that $\mathcal{F}|S \subseteq [S]^{\leq n}$.

Indeed, take any $F\in \mathcal{F}|S$, $F=\{\gamma_\alpha:\ \alpha\in A\}$ and notice that
$$ \frac{1}{n}|F| = \| \frac{1}{n} \chi_F\| \leq \| P_F\Big( \sum_{\alpha\in A} Te_\alpha \Big) \| \leq \| \sum_{\alpha\in A} Te_\alpha \| = \| T(\sum_{\alpha\in A} e_\alpha) \| \leq 1$$
and therefore $|F|\leq n$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- prop-10: body_md -->
Let $\kappa, \lambda$ be uncountable cardinals with $\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)= \lambda$ and let $\mathcal{F} \subseteq [\kappa]^{<\omega}$ be a hereditary family covering $\kappa$.
The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item There is an isomorphic embedding $T\colon c_0(\lambda) \to X_\mathcal F$,
\item There is an operator $T\colon c_0(\lambda) \to X_\mathcal F$ with range of density $\lambda$,
\item There is $S\in [\kappa]^\lambda$ and $n<\omega$ such that $\mathcal F|S \subseteq [S]^{\leq n}$,
\item There is an isomorphic embedding $T\colon \ell_\infty(\lambda) \to Y_\mathcal F$,
\item There is an element $y\in Y_\mathcal{F}$ with $|\operatorname{supp}(y)| = \lambda.$
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-10 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
(5)$\implies$ (3). Let $S_\varepsilon = \{\alpha: |y(\alpha)| > \varepsilon\}$. There exists an $\varepsilon > 0$ with $|S_\varepsilon| \geq \lambda.$ This set works.
\medskip

(3) $\implies$ (5). We have $\|\chi_S\|_\mathcal{F} \leq n$.
\medskip

(3) $\implies$ (4). Take mapping given by $T(e_\alpha) = \chi_{\{S[\alpha]\}}$, where $S[\alpha]$ is the $\alpha$-th element of $S$. This mapping has norm $\leq n$.
\medskip

(4)$\implies$(5) or (3). By a similar argument as in the proof of the previous proposition we can get that $\{\operatorname{supp} (Te_\alpha): \alpha < \lambda\}$ is point countable. Now, we may assume that $|\operatorname{supp}(Te_\alpha)|< \lambda$ (otherwise we get $(5)$). Then for every $\alpha$ the set $\{\xi<\lambda: \operatorname{supp}(Te_\alpha) \cap \operatorname{supp} (Te_\xi) \neq \emptyset\}$ has cardinality less than $\lambda$. So by regularity of $\lambda$ there exists $I \subseteq \lambda$ with $|I|=\lambda$ and \[
\forall \alpha, \beta \in I \, \operatorname{supp}(Te_\alpha) \cap \operatorname{supp} (Te_\beta) = \emptyset,
\] Now we can repeat argument from previous proposition to prove $(3)$.
\medskip
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- rem-3: body_md -->
The implication $(2)\implies (3)$ follows easily from a result of Drewnowski (\cite[Theorem 2]{Drewnowski})
<!-- end rem-3 -->
<!-- cor-3: body_md -->
Let $\kappa, \lambda$ be infinite cardinals with $\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)>\omega$ and let $\mathcal{F} \subseteq [\kappa]^{<\omega}$ be monochromatic.
The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item There is an isomorphic embedding $T\colon c_0(\lambda) \to X_\mathcal F$.
\item There is an operator $T\colon c_0(\lambda) \to X_\mathcal F$ with range of density $\lambda$
\item There is a $0$-monochromatic $S\subseteq \kappa$ of size $\lambda$.
\item There is an isometrically isomorphic embedding $T\colon c_0(\lambda) \to X_\mathcal{F}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end cor-3 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Note that if $S\in [\kappa]^\lambda$ satisfies $\mathcal F|S \subseteq [S]^{\leq n}$, then there is $S'\in [S]^\lambda$ such that $\mathcal F|S' \subseteq [S']^{\leq 1}$ -- otherwise by the Erd\H{o}s--Dushnik--Miller theorem we would find an infinite $A\subseteq S,$ $A\in \overline \mathcal{F}$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- exa-1: body_md -->
Let $S\subseteq \omega_1$ be a Suslin tree and let $c$ be the \emph{comparability} coloring. By Corollary \ref{perfect} we have $X^*_c = Y_{1-c}$. The space $X_c$ does not contain neither $\ell_1(\omega_1)$ nor $c_0(\omega_1)$.
	We will study $X_c$ in Section \ref{sec:Suslin}.
<!-- end exa-1 -->
<!-- exa-2: body_md -->
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be of size $\omega_1$ and fix $\preceq$, a well-ordering of $A$. Define $c\colon [A]^2 \to 2$: for $x<y$ let $c(x,y)=1$ iff $x\preceq y$. Then there are neither uncountable $1$-monochromatic not
	uncountable $0$-monochromatic sets, and so $X_c$ does not contain neither $\ell_1(\omega_1)$ nor $c_0(\omega_1)$. Again, $c$ is perfect (as it is generated by a partial order), and so, by Corollary \ref{perfect} we have $X^*_c = Y_{1-c}$. In \cite{Perfect} the authors considered countable versions of such colorings (in
	this case we take an infinite $A\subseteq \mathbb{Q}$, fix a well-ordering of $A$ and proceed as above). It turned out that despite there are many 'non-isomorphic' countable Sierpi\'nski colorings, all the combinatorial Banach spaces induced by them are
	isomorphic. Probably in the uncountable case this is no longer true.
<!-- end exa-2 -->
<!-- exa-3: body_md -->
In the literature, especially in articles of Erd\H{o}s, Hajnal, Mat\'e, Komj\'ath, one can find a lot of peculiar examples of colorings and graphs, which may be used to for generating interesting Banach spaces. We present here
		two such examples. A graph $G$ on $\omega_1$ is called \emph{Hajnal-Mat\'e} (HM, in short) if the chromatic number of $G$ is $\omega_1$ but for each $\alpha<\omega_1$ the set $\{\eta<\alpha\colon \{\eta, \alpha\} \in E(G)\}$ is finite. Here, $E(G)$
		denotes the set of edges of $G$. Under $\Diamond$ there
		are HM graphs which are even triangle free. Under Martin's Axiom and negation of $\mathsf{CH}$, there are no HM graphs (see \cite{HajnalMate}).
	Because of Theorem \ref{prop:c0} if $G$ is a triangle-free HM graph, $X_G$ is isomorphic to $c_0(\omega_1)$, so it does not produce any new object in the isomorphism category. However, perhaps this renorming of $c_0(\omega_1)$ possesses some
	interesting properties. 

	A graph on (an uncountable cardinal) $\kappa$ is \emph{Erd\H{o}s-Hajnal} if it has a chromatic number $\kappa$ but each of its subgraphs of size less than $\kappa$ has countable chromatic number. An example of an Erd\H{o}s-Hajnal graph on
	$\omega^{\omega_1}$ is the following: connect $f, g\in \omega^{\omega_1}$ by an edge if $\{\alpha\colon f(\alpha)=g(\alpha)\}$ is countable. Again, $X_G$, for $G$ being Erd\H{o}s-Hajnal, may have interesting properties, particularly from the point of view of its subspaces of density less than $2^{\omega_1}$.
<!-- end exa-3 -->
<!-- exa-4: body_md -->
In \cite{Shelah-Steprans} and \cite{Shelah88} the authors considered a hereditary family $\mathcal{F}$ with the property which in our language can expressed in the following way: for every sequence $\{(\xi_\alpha,
	\beta_\alpha)\colon \xi_\alpha \ne \beta_\alpha < \omega_1,
\alpha<\omega_1\}$ and every $k\in \omega$ there is $X \in [\omega_1]^k$ such that $\{\xi_\alpha\colon \alpha\in X\} \in \mathcal{F}$ and $\{\beta_\alpha\colon \alpha \in X\} \in \mathcal{F}^\perp$. The combinatorial Banach spaces induced by this
family is one of the examples of Banach spaces with \emph{few} operators. In the case of \cite{Shelah-Steprans} it particularly means that every operator on the resulting space is a sum of a multiple of identity and an operator with separable range.
<!-- end exa-4 -->
<!-- exa-5: body_md -->
Compact families are particularly important in the case of separable combinatorial Banach spaces. In fact, most of the combinatorial Banach spaces studied in the literature was induced by compact families. The canonical
	example here is the Schreier family $\mathcal{S}$: $S\subseteq \omega$ belongs to $\mathcal{S}$ if $|S|\leq \min S+1$. For $\kappa > \omega$ there is no obvious counterpart of Schreier family. In  \cite{LargeArgyros} Argyros et al consider a
	hereditary family $\mathcal{F}$ on $\omega_1$ which is compact and which is additionally $\alpha$-large, i.e. for every infinite $X\subseteq \omega_1$, the Cantor-Bendixson rank of $\mathcal{F}|X \colon = \{ F\cap X\colon F\in \mathcal{F}\}$ is at least
$\omega^\alpha+1$ (equivalently $ \mathcal{F}|X$ contains a copy of Schreier family of rank at least $\alpha$). 

The authors of \cite{LargeArgyros} used this family to define Banach spaces but in a different spirit than that of our paper: they construct rather a version of Tsirelson space. 

There is also a similar concept: a family $\mathcal{F}$ is \emph{large} if for every $k\in \omega$ and an infinite set $X\subseteq \omega_1$ there is $F\in \mathcal{F}$, $|F|>k$ and $F\subseteq X$.
Note that there is a compact, hereditary, large family on $\kappa$ if and only if $\kappa$ is not $\omega$-Erd\H{o}s cardinal. 

It is worth mentioning that there is a famous open problem if one can define a family of properties similar to Schreier family on $\omega_1$: Fremlin in \cite{Fremlin-DU} asked if there is a family $\mathcal{F}\subseteq [\omega_1]^{<\omega}$ which is compact and
$1/2$-filling, i.e. such that for each $A\in [\omega_1]^{<\omega}$ there is $F\in \mathcal{F}$ such that $|F|>|A|/2$.
<!-- end exa-5 -->
<!-- thm-6: body_md -->
\label{complemented2} For every Banach space $X$ with a monotone unconditional basis of size $\kappa$ there is a hereditary family $\mathcal{F}$ on $\kappa$ such that $X_\mathcal{F}$ contains a complemented isometric copy of $X$.
<!-- end thm-6 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
First, notice that if $X$ is a Banach space with unconditional basis $(e_\alpha)_{\alpha<\kappa}$, then $X^*$ can be treated as a set of sequences of length $\kappa$ and if $\sigma \in X^*$ and $x\in X$, then $\sigma(x) = \langle \sigma, x\rangle
	\colon = \sum_{\alpha<\kappa}
	\sigma(\alpha) x(\alpha)$. The set of functionals is norming, in the sense that
	\begin{equation}
		\|x\| = \sup\{ \langle \sigma, x\rangle\colon \|\sigma\|^* = 1\}. \tag{$\star$}
\end{equation}
Notice that we do not have to take all $\sigma$'s. It is enough to consider those with finite supports and values in a fixed dense subset of $[-1,1]$. In what follows as this fixed subset we will take the set of dyadic rationals, i.e. numbers of the form
$k/2^n$, for $n\in \omega$ and $k\in [-2^n, 2^n]$.

Instead of $\kappa$ we will work with $\Omega = \omega \times \kappa$. Let $I_\alpha = \omega \times \{\alpha\}$. 
	For $\alpha<\kappa$ let $\mu_\alpha$ be the measure on $\Omega$ defined by \[ \mu_\alpha = \sum_n \delta_{\langle n, \alpha\rangle}/2^{n+1}.\] 
Notice that $\mu_\alpha$ is supported on $I_\alpha$. 

Define 
\[ \mathcal{F} = \{ F \in [\Omega]^{<\omega}\colon (\mu_\alpha(F))_\alpha \in B(X^*) \}. \]
Let $x_\alpha(\langle i, \xi\rangle) = 1/2^{i+1}$ if $\xi = \alpha$ and $x_\alpha(\langle i, \xi\rangle) = 0$ if $\xi \ne \alpha$. Then $x_\alpha \in X_\mathcal{F}$ and $\|x_\alpha\|_\mathcal{F} = 1$ for each $\alpha$.

We will show that $T\colon X \to X_\mathcal{F}$ induced by $T(e_\alpha) = x_\alpha$ is an isometric embedding. Let $y \in X$. Since $(e_\alpha)_\alpha$ is monotone, we may assume that $y$ tests positive on all basis functionals. Moreover, as we have
mentioned above, we can
determine its norm (in the sense of ($\star$)) by using only finitely supported functionals with dyadic rational values. Notice that any such functional can be represented as $(\mu_\alpha(F))_\alpha$ for some $F\in \mathcal{F}$. Hence we get  

$$\| Ty \|_\mathcal{F} = \| \sum_{\alpha < \kappa} y(\alpha) x_\alpha \|_\mathcal{F} = \sup_{F\in \mathcal{F}} \sum_{\alpha <\kappa} \mu_\alpha(F) \cdot y(\alpha) = \| y \|.$$ 
The second equality follows from that fact that 
\[ \sum_{\langle n,\beta\rangle \in F} \sum_{\alpha<\kappa} x_\alpha(n,\beta) = \sum_{\alpha<\kappa} \mu_\alpha(F). \]

We will now show that $T[X]$ is complemented in $X_\mathcal{F}$. Define $S\colon X_\mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}^\Omega$ by 
\[ S(x)(n, \alpha) = \frac{1}{2^{n+1}}\int x \ d \nu_\alpha, \]
where $\nu_\alpha$ is a counting measure supported on $I_\alpha$.

Notice that $S$ is linear and $S(x_\alpha) = x_\alpha$ for each $\alpha$. Hence, $S$ is identity on $T[X]$ and $T[X] \subseteq S[X_\mathcal{F}]$. Also, it is not hard to see that $S^2 = S$. It remains to show that $S$ is continuous. It will follow that
$S[X_\mathcal{F}] \subseteq X_\mathcal{F}$ and, in fact, $S[X_\mathcal{F}] \subseteq T[X]$ (if $x\in X_\mathcal{F}$, then  $y: = (\int x \ d\mu_\alpha)_\alpha \in X$, and $S(x) = T(y)$).

Let $x\in X_\mathcal{F}$. We will show that $\| S(x) \|_\mathcal{F} \leq \| x \|_\mathcal{F}$. Indeed, fix $\alpha<\kappa$ and a finite set $F_\alpha \subseteq I_\alpha$. There is a set $G_\alpha \subseteq I_\alpha$ such that
$|G_\alpha| \leq
|F_\alpha|$ and $\int_{G_\alpha} x \ d\nu_\alpha \geq \int_{F_\alpha} S(x) \ d\nu_\alpha$. Using this observation, for every $F\in \mathcal{F}$ one can find $G\in \mathcal{F}$ such that $\sum_{\langle n,\alpha\rangle \in G} |x(n, \alpha)| \geq
\sum_{\langle n,
\alpha\rangle \in F} |S(x)(n, \alpha)|$ and so $\| S(x) \|_\mathcal{F} \leq \| x \|_\mathcal{F}$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- thm-7: body_md -->
\label{complemented} For every Banach space $X$ with a unconditional basis of size $\kappa$ there is a hereditary family $\mathcal{F}$ on $\kappa$ such that $X_\mathcal{F}$ contains a complemented isomorphic copy of $X$.
<!-- end thm-7 -->
<!-- df-1: body_md -->
We say that a family $\mathcal{F}$ of finite subsets of $\kappa$ is a \emph{$\kappa$-universal hypergraph} if for every family $\mathcal{G}$ of finite subsets of $\kappa$ there exists a mapping $\phi:\kappa \xrightarrow[]{} \kappa$ with \[
	A \in \mathcal{G} \iff \phi[A] \in \mathcal{H}.
    \]
<!-- end df-1 -->
<!-- thm-8: body_md -->
Suppose that there is a $\kappa$-universal hypergraph. Then there is a hereditary family $\mathcal{F}$ of finite subsets of $\kappa$ such that $X_\mathcal{F}$ contains a complemented copy of
	every Banach space with unconditional basis of size $\kappa$.
<!-- end thm-8 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a $\kappa$-universal hypergraph and let $\mathcal{F}$ be its hereditary closure (i.e. $\mathcal{F}$ contains all the subsets of elements of $\mathcal{H}$). Then for every hereditary family $\mathcal{G}$ on $\kappa$ there is $\phi \colon \kappa \to \kappa$ such that $\{A\colon \phi[A] \in
	\mathcal{H}\} = \mathcal{G}$. It follows that $\{\phi(\alpha)\colon \alpha<\kappa\}$ generates a complemented copy of $X_\mathcal{G}$ and so $X_\mathcal{F}$ contains a complemented copy of every combinatorial Banach space with density $\kappa$.
	By Theorem \ref{complemented}, in fact
$X_\mathcal{F}$ contains a complemented copy of every Banach space with unconditional basis of size $\kappa$
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- prop-11: body_md -->
Suppose that $\kappa$ is a cardinal satisfying $\forall \lambda < \kappa \; 2^\lambda \leq \kappa$. Then there exists a $\kappa$-universal hypergraph.
<!-- end prop-11 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Let \[
    S = \bigcup_{\alpha < \kappa} \kappa \times \mathcal{P}([\alpha + 1]^{<\omega}).\]
	By assumption on $\kappa$ we conclude that $|S| = \kappa$, so we may construct the $\kappa$-universal hypergraph on $S$.
 Define a family $\mathcal{H}$ of finite subsets of $S$ in the following way \[
	 \{\langle \alpha_1, F_1\rangle, ..., \langle \alpha_n, F_n\rangle \} \in \mathcal{H} \iff \{\alpha_1,...,\alpha_n\} \in F_n,
    \]
where $\alpha_1 < ... < \alpha_n$.

We claim that $\mathcal{H}$ is a $\kappa$-universal hypergraph. Indeed, fix $\mathcal{G} \subseteq [\kappa]^{<\omega}$. Let \[
		\phi_\mathcal{G} (\alpha) = (\alpha, \mathcal{G} \cap \mathcal{P}([\alpha + 1]^{<\omega}).
    \]Let $A = \{\alpha_1 < ... < \alpha_n\}$. Then \begin{align*}
		&\phi_\mathcal{G}[A] \in \mathcal{H} \iff \{(\alpha_1, \mathcal{G} \cap \mathcal{P}([\alpha_1 + 1]^{<\omega}), ..., (\alpha_n, \mathcal{G} \cap \mathcal{P}([\alpha_n + 1]^{<\omega})\} \in \mathcal{H} \iff \\
				& \iff \{\alpha_1, ..., \alpha_n\} \in \mathcal{G} \cap \mathcal{P}([\alpha_n + 1]^{<\omega}) \iff \{\alpha_1, ..., \alpha_n \} \in \mathcal{G} . 
    \end{align*}
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- cor-4: body_md -->
If CH holds, then there exists a $\omega_1$-universal hypergraph and, more generally, if GCH holds, then for every $\kappa$ there exists a $\kappa$-universal hypergraph.
	Also, in ZFC, there exists an uncountable cardinal $\kappa$ with a $\kappa$-universal hypergraph.
<!-- end cor-4 -->
<!-- prop-12: body_md -->
$\mathbb{P}$ is ccc.
<!-- end prop-12 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Let $(p_\alpha)_{\alpha<\omega_1}$ be an uncountable subfamily of $\mathbb{P}$ and denote $F_\alpha = F_{p_\alpha}$, $G_\alpha = G_{p_\alpha}$. Using
	$\Delta$-system lemma we may assume that the family $(\mathrm{supp}(p_\alpha))_\alpha$ forms a $\Delta$-system with a root $\Delta$ and there is $F'$, $G'$ such that $F_\alpha|\Delta = F'$ and $G_\alpha|\Delta 	= G'$ for each $\alpha$.
	For $\alpha, \beta < \omega_1$, $p_\alpha$ and $p_\beta$ are compatible: it follows from the fact that $|F' \cap G'|\leq 1 $ and the supports of $p_\alpha$, $p_\beta$ are disjoint outside of $\Delta$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- thm-9: body_md -->
\label{generic} Let $\dot{\mathcal{F}}$ be the generic family on $\omega_1$ added by forcing $\mathbb{P}$ and let $\mathcal{H}$ be a hereditary family on $\omega_1$ from the ground model. The space $X_{\dot{\mathcal{F}}}$ cannot be embedded into $X_\mathcal{H}$.
<!-- end thm-9 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Suppose that there is $\dot{T}$, a $\mathbb{P}$-name for a function $\dot{T}\colon X_{\dot{\mathcal{F}}} \to X_\mathcal{H}$ such that $1\Vdash$``$\dot{T}$ is an isomorphic embedding''. Denote $\dot{x}_\alpha = \dot{T}(e_\alpha)$ for each $\alpha<\omega_1$. 
                                                                         
	For $k>1$ we say that a condition $p$ $k$-decides $\dot{x}_\alpha$ if there is an interval $I$ of length $1/k$ such that $p\Vdash \| \dot{x}_\alpha \|_{\mathcal{H}} \in I$. 

	Let $p\in \mathbb{P}$. Passing to a stronger condition if needed we may assume that there is $K\in \omega$, $K>1$, such that $p\Vdash 1/K \| x\| < \|T(x)\| < K \| x\|$.
	
For each $\alpha$ fix $p_\alpha \leq p$ such that $p_\alpha$ $K^3$-decides $x_\alpha$. There is an uncountable $\Gamma \subseteq \omega_1$ such that $\mathrm{supp}(p_\alpha)_{\alpha\in \Gamma}$ form a $\Delta$-system with a root $\Delta$ and that
$p_\alpha$'s agree on $\Delta$.

Notice that for each $n$ we can find a set $S\subseteq \Gamma$ such that $|S| = n$ which is free, i.e. for $\alpha\ne \beta \in S$ we have $\alpha \notin \mathrm{supp}(p_\beta)$. Indeed, without loss of generality $(p_\alpha)_{\alpha \in \Gamma}$ are pairwise
different and so the set $\{\min (\mathrm{supp}(p_\alpha)\setminus \Delta) \colon \alpha \in \Gamma\}$ is unbounded. Using this fact it is easy to find the required $S$. Notice also that $S \cap \Delta = \emptyset$.

Find a free $S\subseteq \Gamma$ of size $K^3$ and let $q = \bigcup_{\alpha \in S} p_\alpha$. Then $q$ is a condition. Also, since $q$ $K^3$-decides all $x_\alpha$ in $S$ we have that $q\Vdash \| \sum_{\alpha\in S} x_\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}} < K^2$ or
$q\Vdash \| \sum_{\alpha\in S} x_\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}} > K$:
\medskip

\textbf{Case 1.} $q \Vdash \| \sum_{\alpha \in S} x_\alpha \|_\mathcal{H} < K^2$. Then let $r = (F_q \cup \mathcal{P}(S), G_q)$. Since for every $T\in [S]^2$ we have $T\notin G_q$, $r$ is a condition. But 
\[ r\Vdash \| \sum_{\alpha \in S} e_\alpha \|_{\dot{\mathcal{F}}} = K^3 \mbox{ and } \| \sum_{\alpha \in S} x_\alpha \|_\mathcal{H} < K^2, \]
and so $r\leq p$ forces that $K$ is not appropriate isomorphism constant, a contradiction.
\medskip

\textbf{Case 2.} $q \Vdash \| \sum_{\alpha \in S} x_\alpha \|_\mathcal{H} > K$. Then let $r = (F_q, G_q \cup [S]^2)$. Again, since no element of $[S]^2$ belongs to $F_q$, $r$ is a condition and 
\[ r\Vdash \| \sum_{\alpha \in S} e_\alpha \|_{\dot{\mathcal{F}}} = 1  \mbox{ and } \| \sum_{\alpha \in S} x_\alpha \|_\mathcal{H} > K, \]
which again means that $r\leq p$ forces that $K$ is not a proper constant, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- thm-10: body_md -->
Consistently, there is no $\omega_1$-Pe\l czy\'nski space.
<!-- end thm-10 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
We consider a finite support iteration of length $\omega_2$ of the forcing $\mathbb{P}$ defined above. Let $G$ be the generic.

	We claim that in $V[G]$ there is no $\omega_1$-Pe\l czy\'nski space. Indeed, suppose that $X$ is such a space. Without loss of generality, by Theorem \ref{complemented}, we may assume that $X=X_\mathcal{H}$ for some hereditary family on
	$\omega_1$. As $\mathcal{H}$ is of cardinality $\omega_1$, it appears at an intermediate step $\alpha<\omega_2$ of the iteration. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the family added generically at step $\alpha+1$. By Theorem \ref{generic} $X_\mathcal{F}$
	cannot be embedded isomorphically into $X_\mathcal{H}$, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- thm-11: body_md -->
\label{generic2} Let $\dot{\mathcal{F}}$ be the generic family on $\omega_1$ added by forcing $\mathbb{P}$ and let $\mathcal{H}$ be a hereditary family on $\omega_1$ from the ground model. The space $X_\mathcal{H}$ cannot be embedded into $X_{\dot{\mathcal{F}}}$.
<!-- end thm-11 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
We start as in the proof of Theorem \ref{generic2}. We choose $p$ and, without loss of generality, we assume that there is $K$ such that  $p$ forces that for each $x$, $\|x\|_\mathcal{H}=1$, we have $1/K < \dot{T}(x) < K$. This time we choose
	$p_\alpha$, for each $\alpha$, so that $p_\alpha \Vdash 1/K < \| \dot{x}_\alpha\|_{\dot{\mathcal{F}}} < K$. Also, this time let $S\subseteq \Gamma$ be a free set of size $K^4$.

\textbf{Case 1.} $\| \sum_{\alpha \in S} e_\alpha \|_\mathcal{H} \leq K^2$.
Let $r = (F_q \cup \mathcal{P}(S), G_q)$. Then
\[ r\Vdash \| \sum_{\alpha \in S} \dot{x}_\alpha \|_{\dot{\mathcal{F}}} > K^4/K = K^3 \mbox{ and } \| \sum_{\alpha \in S} x_\alpha \|_\mathcal{H} \leq K^2, \]
and so $r\leq p$ forces that $K$ is not appropriate isomorphism constant, a contradiction.
\medskip

\textbf{Case 2.} $\| \sum_{\alpha \in S} e_\alpha \|_\mathcal{H} > K^2$.
Then let $r = (F_q, G_q \cup [S]^2)$. We have 
\[ r\Vdash \| \sum_{\alpha \in S} \dot{x}_\alpha \|_{\dot{\mathcal{F}}} < K  \mbox{ and } \| \sum_{\alpha \in S} e_\alpha \|_\mathcal{H} > K^2, \]
and so $r$ forces that $K$ is not a proper constant.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- df-2: body_md -->
Let $r>0$. A subset $A$ of a Banach space $X$ is
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{$r$-separated} if $\|x-y\|\geq r$ for every distinct $x,y\in A$.
\item \emph{$r$-equilateral} if $\|x-y\|=r$ for every distinct $x,y\in A$.
\item \emph{equilateral} if there is $s>0$ such that $A$ is $s$-equilateral.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end df-2 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
Let $\alpha\leq \beta < \omega_1$. Then 
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item $p_\alpha \circ p_\beta = p_\alpha|T_{\geq \beta}$.
\item if $s,t\in T_{\geq \alpha}$ and $p_\alpha(s)\neq p_\alpha(t)$, then $s$ and $t$ are incomparable.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
\label{fin-levels-lemma}
    Let $T$ be an $\omega_1$-tree and let $S$ be its uncountable subset. If $p_\alpha[S_{\geq \alpha}]$ is finite for cofinally many $\alpha$'s then $T$ contains a cofinal branch.
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- df-3: body_md -->
Let $T$ be a tree. A pairwise disjoint family $\mathcal{F}\subseteq [T]^{<\omega}$ is \emph{narrow} if for every $A,B\in \mathcal{F}$ there are comparable $a\in A$, $b\in B$. If, additionally, $|A|\leq n$ for each $A\in \mathcal{F}$, then we say that $\mathcal{F}$ is \emph{$(n$-$)$narrow}.
<!-- end df-3 -->
<!-- lem-5: body_md -->
\label{n-proper}
Let $T$ be an $\omega_1$-tree such that there exist an uncountable narrow family $\{F_\alpha:\ \alpha<\omega_1\}\subseteq [T]^{\leq n}$. Then there exists an uncountable $n$-narrow family $\{G_\alpha:\ \alpha<\omega_1\}$ with $G_\alpha\subseteq
T_\alpha$.
<!-- end lem-5 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
By passing to an uncountable subfamily we may assume that for every $\alpha<\beta<\omega_1$ we have $\max ht[F_\alpha] < \min ht[F_\beta]$ and $\min ht[F_0]>0$; in particular $\min ht[F_\alpha]\geq \alpha$ for every $\alpha<\omega_1$. Let $G_\alpha = p_\alpha[F_\alpha]$ for $\alpha<\omega_1$. Clearly $G_\alpha \subseteq T_\alpha$ and $|G_\alpha|\leq |F_\alpha|\leq n$ for $\alpha<\omega_1$, so it is enough to check that $\{G_\alpha:\ \alpha<\omega_1\}$ is narrow. To this end fix $\alpha<\beta<\omega_1$ and pick $a\in F_\alpha$, $b\in F_\beta$ such that $a<b$. Then $a$ and $p_\beta(b)$ are comparable, and therefore $p_\alpha(a)<p_\beta(b)$, which concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lem-6: body_md -->
\label{eqivalent-refolmulation}
Let $T$ be an $\omega_1$-tree and let $\mathcal{F}\subseteq [T]^{<\omega}$ be an uncountable family with $\min(ht[A]) = \max(ht[A])$ for every $A\in \mathcal{F}$. Then the following are equivalent:\begin{enumerate}
        \item $\mathcal{F}$ is narrow,
        \item for every $\alpha<\omega_1$ the family $\{p_\alpha[A]: A\in \mathcal{F}, \min(ht[A]) \geq \alpha \}$ has the intersection property.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-6 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Assume that $\mathcal{F}$ is narrow. Pick $\alpha<\omega_1$ and $A, B\in \mathcal{F}$ such that $ht[A], ht[B]\geq \alpha$. There are $a\in A, b\in B$, which are comparable, and so $p_\alpha(a) = p_\alpha(b)$. Thus, $p_\alpha[A] \cap p_\alpha[B]\neq \emptyset$. 
	Now assume that for every $\alpha<\omega_1$ the family $\{p_\alpha[A]: A\in \mathcal{F}, \min(ht[A]) \geq \alpha \}$ has the intersection property. Pick $A, B\in \mathcal{F}$. We may assume that $A\subseteq T_\alpha, B\subseteq T_\beta$ and $\alpha < \beta$. Then there exists $a \in p_\alpha[A] \cap p_\alpha[B] = A \cap p_\alpha[B]$. So there exists $b \in B$ so that $a = p_\alpha(b)$, but this means that $a < b$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lem-7: body_md -->
\label{transversal-lemma}
	Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a family of finite sets and let $\mathcal{B}$ be a family consisting of finite transversals of $\mathcal{A}$ with size at most $k$. Then either $\mathcal{B}$ is finite or $\mathcal{A}$ has a transversal of size strictly less than $k$.
<!-- end lem-7 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Assume that $\mathcal{B}$ is infinite and let $\mathcal{B} = \{B_i\colon i\in \omega\}$. By the Sunflower Lemma (\cite{ErdosRado1960}) we may assume that there is $R$ such that $B_i \cap B_j = R$ for $i\neq j$. Now note that $|R| < k$ (as
	$(B_i)_i$ are pairwise different) and $R$ is a transversal: if a set $A \in \mathcal{A}$ does not intersect $R$, then it could intersect at most finitely many sets $B_i$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- prop-13: body_md -->
\label{branch}
    Suppose that $T$ is an $\omega_1$-tree that contains a narrow family. Then $T$ has a cofinal branch.
<!-- end prop-13 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Assume that $T$ contains a narrow family $\mathcal{F} = \{F_\alpha\colon \alpha<\omega_1\}$. We may assume that $|F_\alpha| = n$ and for some $n$ and each $\alpha$ and, thanks to Lemma \ref{n-proper}, that $F_\alpha \subseteq T_\alpha.$ Let $m$ be the least
	natural number such that there exists an unbounded set $I\subseteq \omega_1$ and a family $\{ S_\alpha: \alpha\in I\}$ such that for each $\alpha \in I$: \begin{enumerate}
	    \item $|S_\alpha| \leq m,$
        \item $S_\alpha \subseteq T_\alpha$,
        \item $\exists \beta\; \forall \xi > \beta\; p_\alpha [F_\xi] \cap S_\alpha \neq \emptyset.$ (Denote such $\beta$ as $\beta(\alpha).$)
	\end{enumerate}
	It follows from Lemma \ref{eqivalent-refolmulation} that $m \leq n.$ Let $I$ and $\{S_\alpha: \alpha\in I\}$ be as above, and fix $\alpha\in I$. There exists an index $\beta'$ such that for every $\eta \in I \backslash \alpha$ and every $\xi > \beta'$
	we have $p_\alpha[S_\eta] \cap p_\alpha[F_\xi]\neq \emptyset.$ Indeed, it is enough to take $\beta'<\omega_1$ bigger than $\min(\beta(\gamma)\colon p_\alpha(F_\gamma) = p_\alpha[S_\eta\})$ for any $\eta\in I\setminus \alpha$ (it is possible as there are
		only countably many possibilites for $p_\alpha[S_\eta]$). By Lemma \ref{transversal-lemma}, if $\bigcup_{\eta\in I\backslash \alpha} p_\alpha[S_\eta]$ is infinite, then there exists $S'_\alpha$ with cardinality smaller than $m$ that satisfies (2) and 
		(3). Hence, because of the choice of $m$, there
exists $\gamma$ such that for all $\alpha > \gamma$ we have $|\bigcup_{\eta\in I\backslash \alpha} p_\alpha[S_\eta]| < \omega$. By Lemma \ref{fin-levels-lemma} it means that there is a cofinal branch in $T$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- rem-4: body_md -->
It might be an interesting question in finite combinatorics to find, for a given $n$, a maximal size $t(n)$ of $\bigcup \mathcal{F}$ such that $\mathcal{F} \subseteq [\omega]^n$ has the intersection property and does not have transversal
	of size $n-1$ (so, to prove a quantitive version of Lemma \ref{transversal-lemma}).
Notice that if there is a projective plane $P$ of order $n-1$ and $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all the lines on $P$, then $\mathcal{F}\subseteq [\omega]^n$, it has the intersection property, and it does not have a transversal of size $n-1$. Hence, in
this case, $t(n)$ is at least of the size of $P$ and so $t(n) \geq (n-1)^2 + n$. In fact, we conjecture that $t(n) = (n-1)^2 + n$ for every $n$.
<!-- end rem-4 -->
<!-- lem-8: body_md -->
\label{reduction}
Let $(x_\alpha)_{\alpha<\omega_1}$ be a family of vectors in the unit ball of a Banach space $X_\mathcal{F}$. Then for every $\delta>0$ there is an uncountable $\Gamma\subseteq \omega_1$ and vectors $(z_\alpha)_{\alpha\in \Gamma}$ with finite, pairwise disjoints supports and rational values in the unit ball of $X_\mathcal{F}$ such that for every $\alpha<\beta$ in $\Gamma$

$$\|x_\alpha-x_\beta\| - \delta \leq \|z_\alpha-z_\beta\| \leq \|x_\alpha-x_\beta\|+\delta.$$
<!-- end lem-8 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
For $\alpha<\omega_1$ let $y_\alpha$ be a vector with finite support and rational values such that $\|x_\alpha-y_\alpha\|\leq \frac{\delta}{2}.$ Then, clearly, for every $\alpha<\beta<\omega_1$
$$\|x_\alpha-x_\beta\| - \delta \leq \|y_\alpha-y_\beta\| \leq \|x_\alpha-x_\beta\|+\delta.$$

Now pass to an uncountable set $\Gamma\subseteq \omega_1$ such that $(\operatorname{supp}(y_\alpha))_{\alpha<\omega_1}$ is a $\Delta$-system with the root $\Delta$ and $y_\alpha|\Delta = y_\beta|\Delta$ for every $\alpha<\beta$ in $\Gamma$, which is possible since
$y_\alpha$'s have rational values. For $\alpha\in \Gamma$ let $z_\alpha = P_{\omega_1\setminus \Delta} (y_\alpha)$. Then for every $\alpha<\beta$ in $\Gamma$ we have
$$\|z_\alpha-z_\beta\| = \|y_\alpha-y_\beta\|,$$
which completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- thm-12: body_md -->
\label{Aronszajn}
Let $T$ be an $\omega_1$-tree and let $\mathcal{F}$ be the family of finite chains in $T$. Then the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
	\item $T$ is Aronszajn,
\item the unit ball of the space $X_\mathcal{F}$ does not contain an uncountable $(1+\varepsilon)$-separated sets for any $\varepsilon>0$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-12 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
If $T$ contains a cofinal branch $B\subseteq T$, then clearly $\{\chi_{\{b\}}:\ b\in B\}$ is an uncountable $2$-separated set in the unit ball of $X_\mathcal{F}$. Now suppose that $(x_\alpha)_{\alpha<\omega_1}$ is an uncountable $(1+\varepsilon)$-separated
set in the unit ball of $X_\mathcal{F}$ for some $\varepsilon>0$. By Lemma \ref{reduction} we may assume, picking a smaller $\varepsilon>0$ if needed, that $x_\alpha$'s have finite, pairwise disjoint supports and rational values. Also, we may assume that there is $n$
such that $|\operatorname{supp}(x_\alpha)|=n$ for every $\alpha<\omega_1$. For every $\alpha<\beta<\omega_1$ $$\|x_\alpha-x_\beta\|\geq 1+\varepsilon > 1 \geq \max\{\|x_\alpha\|,\|x_\beta\|\},$$
which means that there are comparable $a\in \operatorname{supp}(x_\alpha)$, $b\in \operatorname{supp}(x_\beta)$, i.e. the family $(\operatorname{supp}(x_\alpha))_{\alpha<\omega_1}$ is narrow. Therefore, by Proposition \ref{branch} the tree  $T$ contains a cofinal branch.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- thm-13: body_md -->
\label{Suslin-equilateral}
Let $T$ be an $\omega_1$-tree and let $\mathcal{F}$ be the family of finite chains in $T$. Then the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
	\item $T$ is Suslin,
\item $X_\mathcal{F}$ does not contain an uncountable equilateral set
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-13 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
(2) $\implies$ (1).  Note that if $A\subseteq T$ is an uncountable chain or antichain, then $\{\chi_{\{a\}}:\ a\in A\}$ is an uncountable equilateral set.\medskip

(1)$\implies$ (2). Assume $T$ is a Suslin tree and $X_\mathcal{F}$ contains an uncountable equilateral set. As discussed beforehand, if there is an uncountable equilateral set in $X_\mathcal{F}$, then there is an uncountable $1$-equilateral set $\{x_\alpha:\
\alpha<\omega_1\}$ in the unit sphere of $X_\mathcal{F}$. Apply Lemma \ref{reduction} and pass to an uncountable subfamily to find vectors $(z_\alpha)_{\alpha<\omega_1}$ with finite, pairwise disjoint supports and rational values such that $$0.98\leq
\|z_\alpha-z_\beta\|\leq 1.02$$ for every $\alpha<\omega_1$. We may assume that $r=\|z_\alpha\|$ does not depend on $\alpha<\omega_1$. Let $F_\alpha\subseteq \operatorname{supp}(z_\alpha)$ be a chain such that 
$$r = \sum_{a\in F_\alpha} |z_\alpha(a)|$$
and let $t_\alpha=\max F_\alpha$. Since $T$ is Suslin, the set $\{t_\alpha:\ \alpha<\omega_1\}$ cannot be an antichain, and therefore there are $\alpha<\beta<\omega_1$ such that $t_\alpha$ and $t_\beta$ are comparable, i.e. $F_\alpha \cup F_\beta$ is a chain. For such $\alpha,\beta$ we have 
$$\|z_\alpha-z_\beta\| = 2r\leq 1.02,$$
i.e. $r\leq 0.56$.
However, by Theorem \ref{Aronszajn}, the unit ball of $X_\mathcal{F}$ does not contain an uncountable $(1+\frac{0.38}{0.6})$-separated sets, and so there are $\alpha<\beta<\omega_1$ such that
$$0.98 \leq \|z_\alpha-z_\beta\| < (1+\frac{0.38}{0.6})r,$$
which means that $r>0.6$ -- a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- cor-5: body_md -->
\label{Suslin} If $G$ is a comparability graph of a Suslin tree, then $X_G$ does not contain an uncountable equilateral set.
<!-- end cor-5 -->
<!-- prop-14: body_md -->
\label{MA-equilateral}
Let $\mathcal{F}\subseteq [\omega_1]^{<\omega}$. Then the unit sphere of the space $X_\mathcal{F}$ contains an uncountable equilateral set.
<!-- end prop-14 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Consider the forcing notion $\mathbb P=\mathcal{F}^\perp$ with the order given by reverse inclusion. Clearly, for every $A\in \mathbb P$ we have $\|\chi_A\|=1$.
	Under MA + $\neg$ CH the forcing $\mathbb P$ either contains an uncountable antichain or may be represented as $\mathbb P = \bigcup_{n<\omega} \mathcal A_n$ with each $\mathcal A_n$ closed under finite unions.

If $\mathcal A\subseteq \mathbb P$ is an uncountable antichain, then $\{ \chi_A:\ A\in \mathcal A\}$ is an uncountable $2$-equilateral set. If $\mathbb P = \bigcup_{n<\omega} \mathcal A_n$ with each $\mathcal A_n$ closed under finite unions, then
there is $n<\omega$ and an uncountable $I\subseteq \omega_1$ such that $\{\alpha\}\in A_n$ for every $\alpha\in I$. It follows that $I$ is in the closure of $\mathcal{F}^\perp$, and so $\mathcal{F}|I$ consists of singletons. Hence, $X_\mathcal{F}$ contains an isometric copy of $c_0(I)$ , and therefore an uncountable $1$-equilateral set $\{\chi_{\{\alpha\}}:\ \alpha\in I\}$.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- prop-15: body_md -->
Let $\kappa$ be an infinite regular cardinal, let $T$ be a well pruned $\kappa$-Aronszajn tree. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the family of finite antichains in $T$.
Then the unit sphere of the Banach space $X_\mathcal F$ contains a $(1+\frac{1}{2})$-separated set of size $\kappa$.
<!-- end prop-15 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
We inductively construct sequences $(a_\alpha,b_\alpha,c_\alpha)_{\alpha<\kappa}$ of nodes in $T$ such that:
\begin{itemize}
\item $c_\alpha<a_\alpha,b_\alpha$ for every $\alpha<\kappa$
\item $a_\alpha$ and $b_\alpha$ are incomparable for every $\alpha<\kappa$
\item $\max\{ht(a_\alpha), ht(b_\alpha)\} < ht(c_\beta)$ for every $\alpha<\beta<\kappa$
\end{itemize}

We claim that $(\frac{1}{2}\chi_{\{a_\alpha,b_\alpha\}})_{\alpha<\omega_1}$ form a $(1+\frac{1}{2})$-equilateral set in the unit sphere of $X_\mathcal{F}$.

Indeed, fix $\alpha<\beta<\kappa$. It cannot be the case that both $a_\beta > a_\alpha$ and $b_\beta>b_\alpha$, since we would have that $c_\beta$ is above $a_\alpha$ and $b_\alpha$ at the same time. For the same reason it cannot be the case that both $a_\beta>b_\alpha$ and $b_\beta>a_\alpha$. Therefore the set $\{a_\alpha, b_\alpha, a_\beta, b_\beta\}$ contains an antichain of size 3 and so
$$\|\chi_{\{a_\alpha,b_\alpha\}}- \chi_{\{a_\beta,b_\beta\}}\|\geq 3.$$
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- prob-1: body_md -->
Is there a (natural) property $\varphi$ of a Banach space such that the existence of a Banach space with property $\varphi$ is equivalent to the existence of a Suslin tree?
<!-- end prob-1 -->
<!-- prob-2: body_md -->
Let $X$ be a Suslin space, and let $Y$ be a closed subset of $X$ of density $\omega_1$. Does $Y$ contains an isomorphic copy of a Suslin space?
<!-- end prob-2 -->
